results.project_title: CellLogic: Deep Learning Identification and Characterization of Rare Events in Fluorescent Whole Slide Imaging
results.abstract_text:
Project Summary/Abstract
Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and other rare circulating cells in blood can serve as early warning signs of cancer,
but they are extremely rare and hard to identify – akin to looking for a needle in a haystack. Fluorescent Whole
Slide Imaging (fWSI) now allows researchers to tag these rare cells in patient blood samples, yet the sheer
volume of cells (millions per slide) overwhelms current analysis methods. As a result, valuable information from
these rare cells is often missed with existing technology. We propose to develop an AI-powered image analysis
platform called CellLogic that automatically finds and characterizes rare cells in large fWSI images. CellLogic
uses an unsupervised deep learning model to flag potential rare-cell regions without predefining what the
“needle” looks like (code-named RED), and a downstream single-cell analysis module to precisely segment and
classify each rare cell of interest (code-named BLUE). By removing the need for tedious manual review and
expert-chosen features, this approach can detect unexpected cell types and adapt to multiple cancer
applications, providing a general solution for rare-cell analysis. This fast-track STTR project is a collaboration
between an academic research group and a small biotech company, ensuring that the technology is developed
with a clear path to real-world deployment. In Phase I, we will demonstrate the feasibility and accuracy of the
RED detection module on diverse cancer datasets and build a cloud-based pipeline for high-throughput slide
processing. In Phase II, we will integrate the full rare-cell characterization workflow (RED + BLUE), validate the
platform across multiple laboratory sites, and create user-friendly tools and training resources to support broad
adoption. The expected outcome is a robust, scalable rare-cell analysis tool that can be widely used by
researchers and eventually in clinical diagnostic labs. The success of CellLogic will enable larger multi-site
studies of CTCs and other rare cells, accelerate the discovery of new cancer biomarkers, and improve patient
care by facilitating earlier detection of cancer recurrence and more personalized treatment decisions. In
summary, this project will fill a critical gap in cancer diagnostics by bridging advanced imaging technology
with automated analysis, transforming how we detect and utilize rare cells for improving cancer outcomes.

results.project_title: Optimization and validation of quantitative birefringence microscopy for assessment of myelin pathologies associated with cognitive impairments and motor deficits in young and old aging monkey brain
results.abstract_text:
Degeneration or breakdown of the myelin sheath that wraps and insulates axons of the central nervous system,
as well as peripheral nerves, is a factor in a large array of neurological disorders. These include multiple
sclerosis, stroke, age-related neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, and in non-neurodegenerative age-
related cognitive impairment. To date, myelin breakdown has been assessed indirectly with neurophysiological
assays of conduction, post-mortem myelin staining, or in-vivo diffusion MRI. In the normal aging rhesus monkey,
post-mortem electron microscopy (EM) has confirmed myelin breakdown at the ultrastructural level; however,
EM studies cannot be scaled up to evaluate the entire 100-cc monkey brain or the larger human brain. Myelin
stains suffer from various technical and practical limitations that impede quantification. Other methods, like label-
free spectral confocal reflectance imaging (SCoRe), and coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS), are
promising, but like EM, are expensive, slow and difficult to apply to large brain sections. While SCoRe and CARS
microscopy work in reflectance, opening the possibility of in-vivo imaging through a cranial window in the small-
animal brain, a complementary method is needed that is validated, quantitative and high-resolution, to survey
the status of myelin in whole-brain sections of monkey or human brain. Here we propose to optimize and
validate quantitative birefringence microscopy (qBRM) for high-resolution imaging of normal and
abnormal myelin. The qBRM image provides, for every pixel, two quantitative measures: a) the relative phase
retardance, which is linearly proportional to the density of the birefringent medium and the organization of its
anisotropy; and b) the local orientation of the optic axis of the myelin, which corresponds to the direction of the
structural anisotropy. Archived brain tissues from two rhesus monkey models of myelin damage are available for
this project at the Boston University Medical Campus (BUMC). In Aim 1 we will automate the function of our
birefringence microscope with computer-controlled, motorized polarizer components and stage-positioning, to
facilitate fast, automated image acquisition (montaging) of large tissue sections (up to 40x40 mm). We will also
employ massively-parallel computing resources at BU to rapidly render the multi-megapixel quantitative images.
In Aim 2 we will validate our qBRM image measures by comparing them, in the same sections, with myelin
identified by myelin stains, such as FluoroMyelin Red, and with label-free spectral confocal reflectance (SCoRe)
microscopy. In Aim 3, We will demonstrate the untility of qBRM for quantifying myelin by imaging tissue sections
from three monkey models of myelin pathology: a) behaviorally characterized young and old monkeys with
cognitive assessment; b) behaviorally characterized old monkeys with impaired hand movement produced by
motor-cortex injury and treated with mesenchymal stem-cell derived extracellular vesicles (EVs); c) behaviorally
characterized old monkeys with demonstrated cognitive impairments treated with EVs. Together this will
establish the validity and utility of qBRM for assessing myelin in the central nervous system in health and disease.

results.project_title: Development and validation of a cell separation platform technology
results.abstract_text:
PROJECT SUMMARY / ABSTRACT
The objective of the proposed project is to further develop an enabling, platform technology to help
researchers more easily isolate cells of interest from blood samples. While major feasibility gaps have
already been overcome, additional work on these cell separation devices is required to translate the current
pilot prototype design into a mass-manufacturable embodiment which still retains the unprecedented
capabilities that have been established to date. These include removal of ~99% of red blood cells and
platelets from whole blood samples, as well as the separation of ~95% monocytes and granulocytes from
the lymphocyte / stem cell population. The ability to process standard whole blood draws – rather than
depending on expensive units of mononuclear cells that were harvested via leukapheresis, or the purchase
of frozen aliquots of these units – to acquire the initial starting material with which to perform R&D on
cellular therapies would foster research in the basic, translational, and clinical sciences related to a variety
of blood diseases and disorders. These include, for example, the acquisition of (i) peripheral blood stem
cells in order to perform CRISPR-style research on sickle cell anemia, thalassemia, and other inherited
blood disorders, (ii) monocytes with which to perform extracorporeal photopheresis to investigate or treat
an array of different conditions, including graft versus host disease and cutaneous T cell lymphoma, and
(iii) lymphocytes for the development of adoptive cell-based therapies. The proposed project is aimed at
increasing the readiness level of the novel flow-through cell separation technology described, by first
producing thermoplastic device prototypes, to be manufactured via high-volume commercial techniques,
and then validating in particular their ability to concentrate the CD34+ stem cell population in whole blood
samples by ~100X, while processing an entire 500mL unit of cold-stored whole blood in 2 hours. Single-
use thermoplastic devices will be driven by a basic, off-the-shelf peristaltic pump as with prior prototypes,
which further ensures this platform technology will be amenable to widespread adoption, without the
significant equipment cost expenditure required by existing automated methods. The ‘debulking’ of whole
blood samples, to remove the overwhelming number of interfering cells (largely red cells and platelets) and
enable the selection of rarer cells of interest, while seemingly a simple task is in reality a significant
challenge – one which presently has no ready solution that does not involve undesirable chemical
gradients or lysis steps. A transformative methodology that is wholly different from the inadequate,
currently-available approaches is needed in order to improve the pace and quality of groundbreaking R&D
efforts, and help enable cell-based therapies to fulfill their immense potential.
